cues.text: Watch F1 Finance's Audit Machine prepare the year-end audit of HANGS Construction Services.
It reads the ledger and the statements, and checks that every entry adds up.
It proposes materiality, the size of error that would matter to a reader of the accounts: $340,000.
Then it draws a random sample of thirty bills and checks each against its invoice. Twenty-nine agree.
Next it hunts for unrecorded bills: June work that was paid for after the year end.
It finds four, about $248,000 in all.
Now it tests all 1,261 journal entries, the adjustments made to the books.
Sixteen of them show two or more warning signs.
It checks the warranty reserve, then the dividends against the board's minutes and the bank.
Every dividend agrees with the board and the bank.
Next it ties cash and both loans to the bank's own letter.
The bank confirms both loans, about $4.7 million.
Now it adds up what it found and sets it against materiality.
Then it writes the workpapers and a draft findings memo for the CPA.

All done. Known errors across every area add up to about $560,000, more than materiality, so the CPA asks management to correct them. Recorded in full, they would take net worth about $63,000 below the bank loan's minimum. Seventeen items stay open. The CPA, a person, decides each one and signs. The machine gives no opinion.
